title: Can you prepare for case interviews without a business background?
description: Encouragement and a practical plan for engineers, scientists, doctors, lawyers and anyone new to business who is preparing for case interviews.
hook: If you are an engineer, scientist, doctor, lawyer, teacher or anything other than a business student, case interviews can feel like a test written in someone else's language. Please hear this: firms hire people like you on purpose, and the skills that matter most in a case are ones you have probably already built. What you need is a little vocabulary and a lot of practice, and both are very learnable.
body:
What you already have

  • Structured problem solving. Breaking a problem into parts, forming a hypothesis and testing it is exactly how scientists and engineers work.
  • Comfort with numbers. Case maths is simpler than most technical maths. The challenge is doing it out loud, not the maths itself.
  • Clear communication under pressure. Explaining a diagnosis, presenting research or arguing a case are close cousins of a case recommendation.

What to add

  • Business vocabulary. Start with the consulting glossary and how businesses make money.
  • A few core frameworks. Not to memorise, but to know the usual shapes. Start here.
  • Commercial instinct. Ten minutes a day reading business news and asking "how does this company make money, and what would I do?" builds it faster than you would expect.

Turn your background into an advantage

Interviewers enjoy candidates who bring real experience. A doctor who mentions how hospital beds actually get blocked, or an engineer who knows how factory bottlenecks behave, sounds more credible than a candidate reciting a framework. Use what you know, briefly and when relevant.

In your fit answers

Be ready to explain why you want to move into consulting, in a way that respects your past. Not "I'm leaving medicine because...", but "I loved solving problems for one patient at a time, and I want to work on problems that affect whole systems." Your story is a strength.

A realistic plan

Give yourself a bit more time than business students, ideally six weeks. Spend the first two learning the language and the course, then move quickly into practising full cases. The six-week plan works well.

Translate your existing skills into case performance

A scientist who has designed an experiment already knows how to propose a hypothesis, isolate variables and revise a conclusion. An engineer who has debugged a system already knows how to break a large problem into testable components. The unfamiliar part of a case interview is often the business context, not the underlying reasoning.

Take a small café with falling profit. You do not need an MBA to begin: profit equals revenue minus costs. Revenue can be split into transactions multiplied by spend per transaction. Costs can be split into ingredients, staff, premises and other operating expenses. Ask which line has changed most, then find out why. If transactions fell while ticket size rose, you should investigate footfall or conversion before proposing a price increase.

Try three exercises before memorising terminology. Explain the economics of a business you use every day; turn a news story into a measurable hypothesis; and practise delivering a 30-second recommendation with one number. When you encounter a term you do not know, ask what it means rather than pretending. Curiosity and clarity beat borrowed jargon.
